what_its_for: Escitalopram is used to treat depression and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). It belongs to a group of medicines called SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors), which work by increasing the level of serotonin in your brain. Serotonin is a natural substance that helps improve mood, sleep, appetite, and energy levels.
how_to_take: Take escitalopram by mouth exactly as your doctor prescribed. You can take it with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole with a glass of water. Try to take it at the same time each day — many people find it easiest to take in the morning or at bedtime. Do not crush, chew, or split the tablet unless your doctor tells you it is okay. If you are using the liquid form, use the measuring device provided — never use a regular kitchen spoon.
dosing: The usual starting dose for adults is 10 mg once daily. Your doctor may increase your dose to 20 mg per day after at least one week, depending on how you respond. For older adults (65 and over), the usual dose is 10 mg once daily and should generally not be increased above this. For adolescents (12–17 years), dosing will be determined by your doctor. Always follow your doctor's specific dosing instructions — never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next scheduled dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store escitalopram at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store it in the bathroom medicine cabinet. Keep the bottle tightly closed and out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medication after the expiration date printed on the label. Dispose of unused or expired medication safely — ask your pharmacist about a medicine take-back program near you.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking escitalopram — it can increase drowsiness and make side effects worse. Do not take other antidepressants, especially MAOIs (such as phenelzine or tranylcypromine), within 14 days of taking escitalopram, as this can cause a serious and potentially life-threatening reaction called serotonin syndrome. Be careful when driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you, as it may cause dizziness or drowsiness. Tell all of your doctors and pharmacists about every medication, supplement, or herbal product you take — especially St. John's Wort, blood thinners, pain relievers like aspirin or ibuprofen, and other psychiatric medications.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the nearest emergency room if you experience: thoughts of suicide or self-harm, worsening depression or anxiety, unusual mood or behavior changes (especially in the first few weeks), signs of serotonin syndrome (agitation, confusion, rapid heartbeat, high fever, muscle twitching, loss of coordination), severe allergic reaction (rash, swelling of face or throat, difficulty breathing), seizures, irregular heartbeat or fainting, unusual bleeding or bruising, or low sodium symptoms (headache, weakness, confusion, memory problems). Do not stop taking escitalopram suddenly without talking to your doctor — stopping abruptly can cause withdrawal symptoms such as dizziness, nausea, irritability, and electric-shock-like sensations (called 'brain zaps').
when_it_works: Escitalopram does not work right away — it takes time for your brain chemistry to adjust. Most people begin to notice some improvement in sleep, energy, and appetite within the first 1 to 2 weeks. However, the full benefits for mood and anxiety usually take 4 to 6 weeks of regular use. Some people may need up to 8 to 12 weeks to feel the full effect. Be patient and keep taking your medication as prescribed even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop taking it on your own — always talk to your doctor first.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before taking escitalopram if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Some studies suggest a small risk of heart defects if taken early in pregnancy, and use near delivery may affect the newborn. Your doctor will help you weigh the risks and benefits. Children and teenagers: Escitalopram is approved for use in adolescents aged 12 and older for depression. Young people may have an increased risk of suicidal thoughts when starting antidepressants — watch closely for any changes in mood or behavior and contact the doctor immediately if concerned. Older adults (65+): Older adults are more sensitive to side effects such as dizziness, falls, and low sodium levels (hyponatremia). The recommended maximum dose is usually 10 mg per day. Kidney or liver problems: If you have liver disease, your doctor may start you on a lower dose. Use with caution if you have kidney problems — your doctor will advise you accordingly.
